title: How to keep a simulation library current
summary: Keep simulation content current with an ownership register, policy dependencies, review triggers and a practical process for approving updates.
body_markdown:
A practice exercise can become misleading when the policy, product or workflow changes. Before expanding a simulation library, agree how your team will find affected exercises, review them and withdraw anything that no longer teaches the right behavior.


## Give each exercise an owner and a source


Keep a register that connects each simulation to the process it teaches and the approved material behind it. A title alone is rarely enough to identify every exercise affected by a policy change. Record dependencies such as refund rules, verification requirements and escalation routes in terms the people maintaining those processes recognize.


Separate responsibility for the source policy from responsibility for the exercise. A policy owner confirms what is correct; a training owner checks whether the scenario, learner instructions and assessment still teach it accurately. One person may hold both roles, but neither responsibility should be implicit.


## Use a maintenance register


Use these fields in a spreadsheet or your existing content tracker. The point is a reliable review process, regardless of whether your training platform manages any of it automatically.


Field What to record


Exercise and audience Scenario name, task and assigned learner groups


Approved source Policy owner, document version and relevant dependencies


Review ownership Training owner and person who approves changes


Current status Draft, approved, paused or retired, with the reason


Next review Review date and events that should trigger an earlier check


## Define what happens when something changes


For a routine update, identify affected exercises, revise them and have a reviewer attempt the task before reassignment. Check the expected answer and feedback as well as the scenario wording. For a material error, pause the affected practice while you review it. Tell trainers and learners what changed, especially if someone previously received conflicting guidance.


- Can the owner identify every exercise that depends on the changed rule?
- Do the learner instructions, expected actions and assessment agree?
- Has a reviewer tested a valid approach and a relevant mistake?
- Do existing assignments need updating, and who needs to be notified?


## A fictional example: a changed refund policy


A subscription business introduces an exception for duplicate charges. Its training owner finds exercises covering refunds, billing disputes and cancellation requests in the register. The billing exercise needs a new decision; the cancellation exercise only needs a reference updated. The owner pauses the billing assignment, asks the policy lead to approve the expected behavior and has a trainer attempt both an eligible and an ineligible refund. Learners receive a short explanation before the revised exercise is assigned.


## Budget for maintenance as well as creation


During a pilot, record the time spent locating affected content, making changes, reviewing behavior and updating assignments. Track who supplies that time. A quick edit does not mean a quick release if approval or testing takes longer, and a larger library creates more dependencies to maintain.


Review unused and duplicated exercises before adding more. Retain an exercise because it teaches a relevant task, not because it was expensive to create. Ask any vendor to demonstrate its update workflow with a realistic change; do not assume that connecting a knowledge source also refreshes every exercise or assessment.
